mcqs.question: A graph has 5 edges. What must the sum of all vertex degrees equal?
options: It depends on the number of vertices
mcqs.explanation: The handshake lemma guarantees the sum of degrees always equals 2|E|, regardless of vertex count — here 2×5=10, since every edge adds exactly 1 to each of its two endpoints.

mcqs.question: A citation graph (papers cite other papers) is typically only weakly connected, not strongly connected. Why?
options: Because a directed path rarely exists in both directions between any two papers — citations are one-way in practice
Because it has too many vertices
Because weak connectivity requires fewer edges by definition
Strongly and weakly connected mean the same thing
mcqs.explanation: Strong connectivity requires a directed path each way between every pair; citations flow forward in time (newer papers cite older ones), so a directed path back from an old paper to a newer one essentially never exists, making the graph only weakly connected.

mcqs.question: What does it mean, in terms of cycles, for a graph to be bipartite?
options: It must have no cycles at all
It must contain no odd-length cycle
It must contain no even-length cycle
Bipartiteness has no relationship to cycles
mcqs.explanation: A graph is bipartite exactly when it has no odd-length cycle — an odd cycle forces some edge to connect two same-colored vertices under any 2-coloring attempt, which is precisely what bipartiteness forbids.

mcqs.question: A connected graph has exactly two vertices of odd degree and the rest even. What does this guarantee?
options: It has an Euler circuit
It has a Hamiltonian path
It has an Euler path but not necessarily a circuit
It cannot be traversed at all
mcqs.explanation: Exactly 0 odd-degree vertices gives an Euler circuit; exactly 2 gives an Euler path that must start and end at those two odd-degree vertices (but can't form a closed circuit). Any other odd-degree count rules out both.

mcqs.question: Why is exam scheduling (no student sits two exams at the same time) modeled as a graph coloring problem?
options: Because exams are naturally ordered
It's an analogy with no formal correspondence
Coloring only applies to planar graphs, and exam graphs are planar
Each exam is a vertex, edges connect exams sharing a student, and a valid time-slot assignment is exactly a proper coloring with time-slots as colors
mcqs.explanation: Vertices = exams, an edge means two exams share a student (so they can't be simultaneous), and assigning time slots so no edge connects same-slot exams is exactly graph coloring with slots as colors — the chromatic number is the minimum slots needed.

mcqs.question: Two graphs share the exact same degree sequence. What can you conclude?
options: They might or might not be isomorphic — matching degree sequences is necessary but not sufficient for isomorphism
They are definitely isomorphic
They must have a different number of edges
Degree sequence uniquely determines a graph's structure
mcqs.explanation: Matching degree sequences is only a necessary condition — many non-isomorphic graphs share a degree sequence, since it only counts how many edges touch each vertex, not which vertices actually connect to each other.
